comparison-body: Leon Festinger proposed in 1954 that people judge themselves by comparison with others, and most usefully with others close to them. Herbert Marsh found the other side: measured against a field far above them, capable people rate themselves lower and try less. A top 100 you are nowhere near only discourages; the people one place ahead are a goal.
comparison-title: Social comparison and the big-fish-little-pond effect
comparison-where: Where you see it: if you are outside the top 100 on the leaderboard, "Around your rank" shows you with the two players just above and below you.
credits-intro: Portraits are from Wikimedia Commons. Where no freely licensed photograph exists, the page shows initials instead.
doherty-body: Walter Doherty and Ahrvind Thadani at IBM found in 1982 that people stay engaged and work faster when a computer answers in under about 400 ms. Above it, attention starts to wander.
doherty-where: Where you see it: the site starts loading a page while your pointer is still on its way to the link, or when your finger touches it, and only shows a loading skeleton if a page takes longer than 400 ms.
endowed-body: Joseph Nunes and Xavier Drèze gave car-wash customers loyalty cards. A card needing eight stamps was finished by 19% of people; a card needing ten with two already stamped, the same eight washes, was finished by 34%. A goal that has visibly begun feels worth completing.
endowed-where: Where you see it: the First Week checklist starts with "Create your account" already ticked, because you have done it. The credit is real, never invented.
fitts-body: Paul Fitts showed in 1954 that the time to reach a target grows with its distance and shrinks with its size. Small, far targets are slow to hit.
fitts-where: Where you see it: controls are at least 36px high, and 44px on touch screens. The link prefetcher treats every link as 8px wider on each side when predicting where your pointer is heading.
flow-body: Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi described flow, the absorbed state where challenge sits just above skill: too easy is boredom, too hard is anxiety. Lev Vygotsky said the same about learning decades earlier: the useful exercise is the one you can only just do.
flow-title: Flow and the zone of proximal development
flow-where: Where you see it: the tap-the-beat lesson in RMHMusic speeds up by 8 BPM after a clean run (90 or more) and slows down after a hard one (under 60), between 64 and 96 BPM.
gestalt-body: Max Wertheimer and Kurt Koffka showed that the eye groups what is close together, aligned or enclosed before it reads any detail. Spacing alone says what belongs together; a box around every group is noise.
gestalt-where: Where you see it: Steel separates things with a thin rule or with space instead of boxes, so groups form by nearness and alignment.
goal-body: In 1932 Clark Hull observed that rats in a maze ran faster the closer they got to the food. People do the same: effort rises as a goal comes into view, so the distance left is the most motivating number to show.
goal-where: Where you see it: once a daily or weekly quest is two-thirds done, it says how many are left, such as "2 to go", instead of only "8 / 10".
hick-body: W. E. Hick measured that the time to choose grows with the number of choices. George Miller showed that working memory holds only a handful of items at once; later work puts it nearer four. Fewer, better options are faster to choose from.
hick-where: Where you see it: short lists where a choice is made, such as at most three rows in "Pick up where you left off" and five rows in "Around your rank".
holding-body: The psychoanalyst Donald Winnicott wrote about the holding environment: a calm, reliable setting in which a person feels safe enough to try things. Martin Seligman showed the opposite: when nothing a person does seems to matter, they stop trying. A dead end teaches helplessness; a way forward keeps people going.
holding-title: The holding environment and learned helplessness
holding-where: Where you see it: error pages never blame you and always offer a next step, such as trying again, going home or exploring. Empty states point somewhere, such as "Find people" on an empty friends leaderboard.
intro: A lot of how RMH Studios works comes from a century of psychology research. This page names each idea, the people behind it, what it says, and exactly where you meet it here. It also lists the techniques we have chosen not to use, because the same research can be turned against the people it describes.
jung-body: Carl Jung described archetypes: recurring figures such as the wise old man, the trickster and the hero that appear in stories everywhere and that people recognise at once. A character built on one reads as a person rather than a list of traits.
jung-where: Where you see it: every AI account in the feed is built around one archetype (the Sage, the Trickster, the Hero, the Caregiver, the Child or the Wanderer), which keeps its voice consistent from post to post. AI accounts always carry an Automated badge.
labor-body: Michael Norton and colleagues found that people value a result more when they can see the work behind it, even when it takes longer, and that people value what they helped build, from flat-pack furniture to origami, more than the same thing made for them. The work shown must be the real work.
labor-title: The labor illusion and the IKEA effect
labor-where: Where you see it: while "Ask the feed" works, it says what it is doing (searching public posts and reading up to 60 of them), and afterwards how many posts it read. Profile customisation and User Builds rest on the IKEA effect.
loss-body: Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky showed that a loss weighs about twice as much as an equal gain. A reminder framed as "you are about to lose your streak" is the strongest lever a site has, and it works by making people anxious.
loss-where: What we do: the streak reminder states the fact ("Your 7-day streak continues if you check in today") with no fire emoji, no countdown and no threat. Freeze tokens cover days you miss.
peakend-body: Daniel Kahneman and colleagues found that people judge an experience mostly by its most intense moment and by how it ended, not by its average or its length. The end of a game is the part you carry away, so it should show the best of the run.
peakend-where: Where you see it: the game-over screens of Void Breaker, Neon Driftway and Nightrail lead with your best moment of the run, such as your longest combo or closest calls, before the full table of numbers.
restorff-body: Hedwig von Restorff found in 1933 that an item that differs from everything around it is the one people remember. One distinct button marks the main action; two distinct buttons cancel each other out.
restorff-where: Where you see it: each view has one solid ink button for its main action; everything else is outlined or plain.
sdt-body: Edward Deci and Richard Ryan showed that lasting motivation rests on three needs: autonomy, competence and relatedness. Mark Lepper's overjustification studies added a warning: paying people for something they already enjoy can make them enjoy it less. Feedback that tells you that you got better keeps play its own reward.
sdt-where: Where you see it: when a run beats your record, the game-over screen tells you by how much. That line reports your skill; it is not a payout.
section-avoid: What we choose not to do
section-avoid-intro: The same research can make a product harder to put down without making it better. These are the techniques we leave out.
section-design-intro: The perception research behind the Steel design and the site's performance work.
section-play-intro: How the site helps you finish things and keeps practice worth doing.
section-social-intro: How the site compares you with others, and the people it creates.
skinner-body: B. F. Skinner found that rewards delivered at unpredictable intervals produce the most persistent behaviour of any schedule. It is the mechanism of slot machines and endless feeds, which is exactly why we do not spread it through the site.
skinner-where: What we do: we add no new random rewards. The spinning wheel and the casino games are the only ones, and they stay where you choose to go to them.
spacing-body: Hermann Ebbinghaus memorised thousands of nonsense syllables and measured how fast he forgot them. Memory fades on a steep curve, and each well-timed review flattens it, so reviews spaced further and further apart keep material with the least effort.
spacing-title: The forgetting curve and spaced repetition
spacing-where: Where you see it: RMHStudy decks and RMHMusic practice schedule each card for the moment you are about to forget it.
subtitle: The research behind how this site behaves, and the people who did it.
title: Psychology
weber-body: Ernst Weber and Gustav Fechner found that the smallest change people notice is a fixed fraction of what is already there, not a fixed amount. A page that loads 100 ms faster feels very different at 300 ms and not at all at 5 seconds.
weber-where: Where you see it: the site's performance budget reports every change as a percentage of the whole page, because the same number of kilobytes matters more on a small page than on a large one.
zeigarnik-body: In 1927 Bluma Zeigarnik noticed that waiters remembered unpaid orders far better than paid ones, and showed in the lab that people recall interrupted tasks about twice as well as finished ones. An unfinished task keeps a small claim on attention until it is done.
zeigarnik-where: Where you see it: "Pick up where you left off" at the top of the home feed lists up to three unfinished things: a game save, a book, a draft, a deck with cards due.
